draft.title: First Nations voices and context
card: First Nations Australian authors write from the experience of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Their works are read with the context in mind: the histories, cultures and communities the author speaks from.
Connection to Country is a central idea in many First Nations works. Country means the land, waters and sky, and the ties of kin, culture and responsibility to them. It is more than a setting.
First Nations peoples have the right to tell their own stories. A work by a First Nations author gives a view from inside a community, not a view from outside.
Knowing the context helps a reader see why an author chose certain events, images or language. It does not mean every First Nations author says the same thing. Each voice is individual.
draft.remember: Read First Nations works with their context in mind: history, Country and the right to tell your own story.

a.q: Why does a reader consider context when reading a work by a First Nations author?
opts: It helps explain the histories the author writes from
It shows that all First Nations authors share one view
It lets readers swap the author's meaning for their own
It makes the text's language and structure matter less
a.why: Context helps a reader see the histories, culture and Country that shape the author's choices. It does not mean authors share one view, because each voice is individual.
a.clue: Context helps you see where the author is speaking from.

b.q: Priya reads a poem by a First Nations author in which a river is spoken of like a relative. What is the best way to read the river?
opts: As a sign of kinship and responsibility to Country
As a plain backdrop with no link to the speaker
As a symbol that stands for the poet's own wealth
As a decoration chosen only to make the poem rhyme
b.why: In many First Nations works, Country includes waters and carries ties of kin and responsibility, so a river can be read as a relative. Treating it as only a setting misses this context.
b.clue: Think about what Country means beyond a setting.

a.best: It helps explain the histories the author writes from

b.best: As a sign of kinship and responsibility to Country

problems.detail: "A work by a First Nations author gives a view from inside a community, not a view from outside" is too absolute. Some First Nations authors write about communities that are not their own, or from experiences of separation from community, such as the Stolen Generations. This also sits uneasily with the card's own point that each voice is individual. Soften it to "can give" or "often gives".

"The right to tell your own story" switches to "your", so it reads as if it is about the student's right. The card says First Nations peoples have the right to tell their own stories. Use "their own stories".
The clue "Think about what Country means beyond a setting" points to the only option that contains the word Country. It also rules out the backdrop option, so it gives the answer away.
